chapters.title: Chapter 4: Valuing a Business on Its Own Cash Flows

lessons.title: Asset-Based Valuation: When Net Worth Is the Right Answer

children.text: A textile mill outside Tiruppur has lost money for six years. A DCF of its cash flows produces a small number, and a peer multiple applied to negative EBITDA produces nothing at all. Yet three buyers are interested and the family expects a high price. The reason sits under the factory: fourteen acres bought in 1985, when the area was farmland and is now inside the city. For this company, the earnings methods answer the wrong question.

body.text: The asset approach values what a company owns rather than what it earns. It is the right answer whenever the assets are worth more than the business standing on them, or when the business is ending rather than continuing.

children.text: Three Different Asset Numbers
Every balance sheet already carries one asset-based figure:
book net asset value
. It is almost never the answer, because accounting records assets at what was paid for them, less depreciation, not at what they are worth today.

markDefs.definition: Total assets less total liabilities, as recorded in the accounts. Also called net worth or shareholders' funds.

body.caption: The starting point. The work lies in restating each line to the right basis
Which asset figure answers which question

cells: Assets at historical cost less depreciation
A starting point only, and a floor that is often badly out of date
Each asset restated to what it would fetch in an orderly sale, with liabilities restated too
Holding companies, asset-heavy businesses, and financial reporting
A forced or time-bound sale, net of the costs of selling
Insolvency, shutdowns, and as an absolute floor in any negotiation

body.text: Land is the usual culprit. Under Indian accounting practice most companies carry land at historical cost, so a plot bought in 1985 for ₹4 crore still sits at ₹4 crore in the books, whatever the market says. Book net worth for an old manufacturing company is frequently the least useful number on the page.

children.text: Worked Example: Palladam Mills
Palladam Mills Private Limited is a fictional loss-making textile company. Here is its balance sheet, then the same assets restated two different ways.

body.caption: Palladam Mills: three views of the same company (₹ crore)

body.title: Palladam Mills: net asset value on three bases

body.text: The audited net worth says ₹25 crore. An orderly sale of the same assets says about ₹114.2 crore. A forced sale says ₹59 crore. All three are honest answers to three different questions, and the one that matters depends entirely on what is about to happen to this company.

children.text: Notice how each line moved, because the reasoning behind each adjustment is what a buyer will test.
Land rose sharply.
Held at 1985 cost, now surrounded by the city. A registered valuer for land and buildings would support the revised figure with comparable sale instances.
Plant fell hard.
Textile machinery is specialised, and second hand buyers are few. Book value assumed a useful life that the resale market does not honour.
Inventory took a haircut.
Finished fabric sells at a discount when the seller is under pressure, and some of it is slow moving.
Receivables took a smaller one.
Some customers will dispute or delay once they hear the company is being sold or wound up.
Liabilities did not move.
Lenders, creditors and employees are owed what they are owed, regardless of which valuation basis you choose.

body.title: Restate a balance sheet
body.prompt: A company has book assets of ₹150 crore and liabilities of ₹90 crore. A valuer finds that land carried at ₹10 crore is worth ₹70 crore, and that plant carried at ₹40 crore would realise only ₹25 crore. No other line changes. What is the fair value net asset value, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Adjusted assets = ₹150 crore + ₹60 crore uplift on land - ₹15 crore write-down on plant = ₹195 crore. Less ₹90 crore of liabilities gives ₹105 crore, against a book net worth of ₹60 crore. One revaluation of land nearly doubled the answer, which is exactly why asset-heavy companies are never valued off the printed balance sheet.

children.text: When the Asset Approach Is the Right Approach

body.caption: Where assets, not earnings, carry the value

cells: The earnings are negative, the land is not
Holding company owning stakes in other businesses
It has no operations of its own, only investments
Net asset value of the stakes, then a holding company discount
Value sits in individual projects and land bank, not in one year of profit
Net asset value of the project pipeline
The question is what creditors can recover
Fair value and liquidation value, both
The assets are financial and observable
Mark to market net asset value
There is no going concern to value

body.title: Pick the method
body.question: Four companies need valuing. Which one is the strongest candidate for an asset-based approach?
options: A software services company growing 20% a year with almost no fixed assets
A profitable FMCG brand with strong distribution and a 40 year old trademark
A holding company whose only assets are minority stakes in three listed group companies
A hospital chain with rising patient volumes and stable margins
body.explanation: The holding company has no operations of its own. Its value is the market value of the stakes it holds, less a discount. The other three are going concerns whose value comes from earnings, and for the FMCG brand in particular an asset approach would badly understate value, since an internally generated brand does not appear on the balance sheet at all.

children.text: Holding Companies and the Indian Discount

An Indian holding company owning listed stakes looks like the easiest valuation in the world. Add up the market value of the stakes, subtract debt, done. The market disagrees, consistently and by a lot.

body.label: What Indian holding companies trade at
body.value: Commonly 40% to 60% below the value of their stakes
body.context: Bajaj Holdings, the largest listed holding company, was reported trading at about a 48% discount to the value of its stakes in group companies, and Tata Investment Corporation has historically traded at a 50% to 60% discount to net asset value. Global holding company discounts are usually nearer 30% to 40%.

children.text: The discount is not irrational. It reflects four things a buyer of the holding company cannot escape.
Cash reaching you passes through two layers, and tax and costs are incurred on the way up
You cannot force the holding company to sell a stake or distribute the proceeds
The holding company's own capital allocation decisions are outside your control
Holding company shares are often thinly traded, which is its own discount

body.title: Compute the discount
body.prompt: A listed holding company owns stakes in group companies with a combined market value of ₹34,000 crore, has no debt, and its own market capitalisation is ₹8,000 crore. What discount to net asset value is it trading at, as a percentage? Round to the nearest whole number.
body.explanation: 1 - (₹8,000 crore ÷ ₹34,000 crore) = 1 - 0.235 = about 76%. That is wide even by Indian standards. Before concluding it is cheap, ask the obvious questions: can anything force the value out, is there a buyback or dividend policy, and how liquid is the stock? A discount that has persisted for a decade may simply be the market's standing answer.

children.text: Asset Valuation in Indian Insolvency

The one place Indian law requires both an orderly and a forced sale number is insolvency. Under the corporate insolvency resolution process regulations, the resolution professional appoints two registered valuers to estimate asset-wise fair value and liquidation value after physically verifying the inventory and fixed assets.

stats.label: Valuers appointed
stats.context: Three if the first two estimates differ significantly

stats.label: How the figure is set
stats.value: Average of the two closest estimates
stats.context: For each of the two values separately

body.text: Liquidation value matters enormously in an insolvency, because it is the floor a resolution plan is measured against. Dissenting creditors are entitled to at least what they would have received in a liquidation, so the estimate produced by two valuers shapes what every bidder must offer.

columns.label: Fair value
points: Assumes an orderly transaction with a willing buyer and seller
Allows reasonable time for marketing the assets
Assets can be sold as a going concern or as a cohesive block
Generally the higher of the two figures

columns.label: Liquidation value
points: Assumes the business is wound up and assets sold piecemeal
Time-bound, often with a compressed sale window
Net of the costs of realisation, and the floor for any resolution plan

children.text: Where the Asset Approach Fails
Used on the wrong company, this method produces an answer that is confidently and badly low.

body.title: What a balance sheet never shows you

children.text: Internally built brands.
A brand a company created itself is not recorded as an asset. Only a brand it bought from someone else appears.
Customer relationships and contracts.
A twenty year relationship with a large buyer has no line in the accounts.
Trained teams and know-how.
The most valuable part of a services business walks out of the building every evening.
Distribution reach.
The reason an acquirer pays a premium for a consumer brand is rarely on the balance sheet.
Licences and approvals.
A hard-won regulatory approval may be carried at the cost of the application fee.

This is why Hindustan Unilever paid ₹2,955 crore for Minimalist, a figure no net asset calculation would ever have produced. For a profitable going concern with intangible strengths, the asset approach sets a floor, not a value.

body.title: The mill and the land
body.scenario: You advise a Tiruppur family whose textile mill has lost money for six years. The mill sits on 14 acres bought in 1985, now inside the municipal limits. Book net worth is ₹25 crore. A property consultant estimates the land alone at ₹120 crore. The elder brother wants to sell the whole company to a competitor who has offered ₹70 crore for 100% of the shares. The younger brother wants to shut the mill, sell the land and distribute the proceeds. Forty workers have been with the family for over twenty years.
body.prompt: Lay out the analysis the family needs before deciding.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Value the company three ways and put all three on one page: as a going concern (a DCF, which will be weak), on fair value net assets (driven by the land), and on liquidation value (the land at a distressed price, less closure costs).
2. Recognise what the ₹70 crore offer really is. It is well above book net worth but far below the land value alone. The competitor is almost certainly buying the land and treating the mill as incidental. Ask whether the offer is for the shares or for the business and assets, because the two are taxed very differently and carry different liabilities.
3. Cost the shutdown route honestly. Closing a mill means employee dues, gratuity, notice and retrenchment obligations, clearing secured lenders, and the time and cost of converting and selling land, including any change of land use approvals. The gross ₹120 crore is not what the family receives.
4. Check what the land can legally be used for. Permitted use, zoning and conversion approvals decide whether ₹120 crore is realistic or aspirational. Get a registered valuer's report on land and buildings rather than relying on a broker's estimate.
5. Model the tax outcome of each route. A share sale, an asset sale by the company followed by distribution, and a slump sale of the business all leave the family with different amounts in hand. This is the single largest swing factor and it needs specialist advice.
6. Address the workers explicitly, both because it is a real obligation and because it affects value. A buyer taking over the workforce prices that in. A closure means the family funds it.
7. Only then negotiate. With three valuations, a tax comparison and a clear closure cost, the family can tell the competitor exactly why ₹70 crore does not clear the floor set by the assets.

body.title: The floor
body.textWithBlank: In an insolvency, a resolution plan is measured against the ___ value, because dissenting creditors must receive at least what they would have got if the company were wound up.
body.explanation: Two registered valuers estimate both fair value and liquidation value asset-wise, and the average of the two closest estimates is taken for each.

body.title: Running an asset-based valuation
steps: List every asset and liability from the latest balance sheet, then ask which are recorded at stale cost
Get land and buildings valued by a registered valuer for that asset class, with comparable sale instances
Value plant and machinery separately, on both a going concern and a second hand basis
Discount inventory for obsolescence and slow movement, and receivables for ageing and disputes
Add liabilities the balance sheet understates: unfunded gratuity, disputed taxes, contingent claims
Check for assets not on the balance sheet at all, such as internally built brands, and note that this method ignores them
Decide the basis: orderly sale or forced sale, and state it clearly in the conclusion
For a holding company, apply and justify the holding company discount rather than importing a standard number
Compare the result against an earnings-based valuation, and treat the higher as the going concern answer only if the business genuinely continues

body.label: IBBI: registered valuers
body.description: Registered valuers are enrolled by asset class: land and building, plant and machinery, and securities or financial assets. Check that the valuer signing a report is registered for the class of asset actually being valued.

cards.definition: Total assets less liabilities as recorded in the accounts, at historical cost.
The same calculation after restating each asset and liability to what it would fetch in an orderly transaction.
What assets realise in a forced, time-bound sale, net of the costs of selling.
What it would cost to recreate an asset of the same utility today, adjusted for obsolescence.
The reduction applied to the value of stakes held by a holding company, commonly 40% to 60% in India.
A valuer enrolled with the IBBI for a specific asset class, required for many valuations under Indian law.
A business expected to continue operating, valued on its earnings rather than its assets.

points: The asset approach values what a company owns. It is right when assets are worth more than the business on them, or when the business is ending.
Palladam Mills showed ₹25 crore of book net worth, about ₹114.2 crore on fair value and ₹59 crore in a forced sale. All three were honest answers to different questions.
Land carried at historical cost is the single biggest reason book net worth misleads for older Indian manufacturers.
Indian holding companies commonly trade 40% to 60% below the value of their stakes, with Bajaj Holdings reported at about 48% and Tata Investment historically at 50% to 60%.
In insolvency, two registered valuers estimate fair value and liquidation value asset-wise, and the average of the two closest estimates is used.
Liquidation value is the floor for a resolution plan, and a useful floor in any negotiation.
Balance sheets ignore internally built brands, customer relationships and trained teams, so the asset approach understates a healthy going concern.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Palladam Mills and the family situation are fictional. Holding company discounts cited are from published market commentary at the time stated and change with prices. Insolvency and valuation requirements are summarised in outline and any real matter needs a registered valuer and legal advice.
